new.title: Tour the Palais des Ducs and its Musée des Beaux-Arts
new.desc: The Palace of the Dukes and Estates of Burgundy was begun in 1364 and mixes Gothic and classical wings. Its east wing holds the Musée des Beaux-Arts, created in 1787 and among the oldest museums in France, with the ducal kitchens and the guard room.
new.tip: Allow two hours for the museum; the same palace houses the town hall and tourist office on Place de la Libération.
new.q: Palais des ducs et des États de Bourgogne, Place de la Libération, Dijon

new.title: Stroke the lucky owl on Notre-Dame de Dijon
new.desc: A small owl is carved on a buttress of the Gothic church of Notre-Dame on rue de la Chouette, worn smooth by generations of hands. Tradition says to stroke it with the left hand while making a wish.
new.tip: Look up at the Jacquemart clock automaton on the facade at the same time. The owl is on the side street, not on the main facade.
new.q: Chouette de Dijon, Rue de la Chouette, Dijon

new.title: Admire the timber-framed Maison Millière
new.desc: This Gothic half-timbered house at 10 rue de la Chouette dates from the late 15th century, built for the merchant Guillaume Millière. It has been a listed monument since 1943 and its roof carries carved animal figures including a cat and an owl.
new.tip: It now houses a restaurant, wine bar and tea room with a small inner garden, so you can step inside for a drink.
new.q: Maison Millière, 10 Rue de la Chouette, Dijon

new.title: Walk the Rue des Forges past the Hôtel Chambellan
new.desc: Rue des Forges is Dijon's old pedestrian main street, lined with noble townhouses from the Gothic to the 17th century. The Hôtel Chambellan at no. 34 has a spiral staircase courtyard, and the Hôtel Aubriot at no. 40 is a 13th-century house with a glazed-tile roof.
new.tip: Courtyards are mostly closed but some open during the Journées du patrimoine; peek through the doorways.
new.q: Rue des Forges, Dijon

new.title: Descend into the Saint-Bénigne crypt and rotunda
new.desc: Dijon cathedral stands over the remains of the Romanesque rotunda built by William of Volpiano and consecrated in 1018. Only its crypt survives, restored between 2020 and 2024 with a pair of striking capitals beside the tomb of Saint Bénigne.
new.tip: Check the cathedral or tourist office for crypt opening hours, which are limited.
new.q: Cathédrale Saint-Bénigne, Place Saint-Bénigne, Dijon

new.title: Study the Renaissance facade of Église Saint-Michel
new.desc: A Gothic church whose west front was given an ornate Renaissance facade in the 16th century, layering Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders. The two towers were added in the 17th century and the church has been a historic monument since 1840.
new.tip: The square in front is a lively evening spot with bars and restaurants.
new.q: Église Saint-Michel, Place Saint-Michel, Dijon

new.title: See Sluter's Well of Moses at Champmol
new.desc: The Puits de Moïse is the surviving base of a calvary made by Claus Sluter for the Chartreuse de Champmol and completed in 1405. Six prophet statues surround the well, which was classified a historic monument in 1840.
new.tip: The site sits inside a psychiatric hospital campus and is visited by guided tour only; book through the Dijon tourist office.
new.q: Puits de Moïse, Chartreuse de Champmol, 1 Boulevard Chanoine Kir, Dijon

new.title: Explore the Cité internationale de la gastronomie et du vin
new.desc: Opened on 6 May 2022 on the site of the former general hospital founded in 1204, this 6.5-hectare complex celebrates the UNESCO-listed French gastronomic meal. It offers exhibitions, workshops and tasting trails, and hosts the International Organisation of Vine and Wine.
new.tip: Wine tasting stations let you sample many Burgundy appellations by the glass.
new.q: Cité internationale de la gastronomie et du vin, Rue de l'Hôpital, Dijon

new.title: Pause at the polar bear in Jardin Darcy
new.desc: Dijon's first public garden, laid out in 1880 above the water reservoir engineered by Henri Darcy in 1838. At the entrance stands a 1937 copy of François Pompon's Ours blanc, next to the Porte Guillaume gate.
new.tip: Free and central; combine it with the Pompon sculptures in the Musée des Beaux-Arts.
new.q: Jardin Darcy, Place Darcy, Dijon

new.title: Visit the Hospices de Beaune and its glazed roofs
new.desc: The Hôtel-Dieu was founded in 1443 by Nicolas Rolin and Guigone de Salins as a charity hospital. Its courtyard is famed for polychrome glazed-tile roofs in geometric patterns, and the Hospices still own vineyards sold at an annual November auction.
new.tip: Book a visit with audioguide or a guided tour at 2 rue de l'Hôtel-Dieu; go early to avoid coach groups.
new.q: Hôtel-Dieu Hospices de Beaune, 2 Rue de l'Hôtel-Dieu, Beaune

new.title: Tour the Château du Clos de Vougeot
new.desc: A Cistercian wine estate and headquarters of the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin. The visit covers the old winemaking halls, the Grand Cellier and the monks' dormitory, and a film on the brotherhood.
new.tip: Wine is not sold on site; book the visit ahead on the official site.
new.q: Château du Clos de Vougeot, Rue de la Montagne, Vougeot

new.title: Stand beneath the medieval castle of Gevrey-Chambertin
new.desc: The fortified château in the village centre was a stronghold built for the abbots of Cluny and reworked in the 13th century. Gevrey-Chambertin is the Côte de Nuits village with the most grand crus on the Route des Grands Crus.
new.tip: Check the village tourist office for guided visits; the vineyard walk behind the village gives the best views.
new.q: Château de Gevrey-Chambertin, Rue du Chambertin, Gevrey-Chambertin

new.title: See the Life of the Virgin tapestries in Beaune
new.desc: The Collégiale Notre-Dame keeps five Tournai tapestries completed around 1500 that tell the life of the Virgin. They are laid out for viewing in the choir during the season.
new.tip: Tapestry viewings run on set afternoons from mid-April to October; confirm times with Beaune tourism.
new.q: Collégiale Notre-Dame de Beaune, Place du Général Leclerc, Beaune

new.title: Climb the fortress village of Châteauneuf-en-Auxois
new.desc: A medieval castle on a rocky spur above the plain, in a village listed among the most beautiful villages of France. The self-guided visit covers military architecture and aristocratic living quarters.
new.tip: Open daily except Monday; combine with a walk along the Canal de Bourgogne below.
new.q: Château de Châteauneuf, Châteauneuf-en-Auxois

new.title: Wander the Cistercian Abbaye de Fontenay
new.desc: Founded around 1118 by Bernard of Clairvaux and inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1981, Fontenay is among the oldest surviving Cistercian abbeys. The church, cloister, dormitory, chapter house and great forge are all visitable.
new.tip: A full visit takes about an hour plus the gardens; the abbey is about 5 km from Montbard station.
new.q: Abbaye de Fontenay, Marmagne

new.title: Relive the siege of Alésia at the MuséoParc
new.desc: The museum on Mont Auxois covers the 52 BC siege where Caesar defeated Vercingétorix, with reconstructions of the Roman fortifications and the excavated Gallo-Roman town. A statue of Vercingétorix erected under Napoleon III stands on the hilltop.
new.tip: Buy tickets online at alesia.com; children under 7 enter free.
new.q: MuséoParc Alésia, 1 Route des Trois Ormeaux, Alise-Sainte-Reine

new.title: Cross the Pont Joly to the towers of Semur-en-Auxois
new.desc: A medieval town on a pink granite spur ringed by the Armançon. The 44-metre Tour de l'Orle d'Or belongs to the old ramparts, the Pont Joly dates from the 1780s, and the Gothic Collégiale Notre-Dame was restored by Viollet-le-Duc.
new.tip: The best photo of the town is from the Pont Joly looking up at the keep and ramparts.
new.q: Tour de l'Orle d'Or, Rue de la Liberté, Semur-en-Auxois

new.title: Read the walls of the Château de Bussy-Rabutin
new.desc: The château was decorated by Roger de Rabutin, a cousin of Madame de Sévigné, with portraits and satirical captions after his exile from court. It stands in a 34-hectare park with a hedge maze and is run by the Centre des monuments nationaux.
new.tip: Guided visits run through the season; the drive from Dijon takes about 55 minutes.
new.q: Château de Bussy-Rabutin, 12 Rue du Château, Bussy-le-Grand

new.title: Meet Pompon's bear and Saint-Andoche in Saulieu
new.desc: The Romanesque Basilique Saint-Andoche has historiated 12th-century capitals, and the neighbouring Musée François Pompon honours the animal sculptor born in Saulieu. A walking trail in the town follows the footsteps of the Ours blanc.
new.tip: Pair the visit with the town's bronze bull monument to Pompon.
new.q: Basilique Saint-Andoche, Place de la Basilique, Saulieu

new.title: Join a guided visit of the Abbaye de Cîteaux
new.desc: The mother house of the Cistercian order, founded in 1098, is still home to a monastic community. Guided tours enter the cloister enclosure, where only the 13th-century library is open to the public, and a film shows monastic life.
new.tip: Booking is strongly advised for the guided visit of about 1h15; the abbey shop is on site.
new.q: Abbaye de Cîteaux, Saint-Nicolas-lès-Cîteaux

new.title: Stand in the ruins of Cluny Abbey
new.desc: Cluny III, begun in 1088 under Abbot Hugues de Semur, was for centuries the largest church in Christendom. The remaining south transept, the 13th-century Farinier with its capitals, and the museum recall its power.
new.tip: Last entry is 45 minutes before closing; the ticket includes the Art and Archaeology museum.
new.q: Abbaye de Cluny, 6 Rue Mercière, Cluny

new.title: Step into the Romanesque Abbaye Saint-Philibert in Tournus
new.desc: Monks arrived in 875 with the relics of Saint Philibert; the abbey church was built mainly between the 10th and 12th centuries. It has a crypt, the Saint-Michel chapel, a cloister and medieval floor mosaics showing the zodiac.
new.tip: Entry to the church is free; audioguides can be rented at the tourist office.
new.q: Abbaye Saint-Philibert, Place de l'Abbaye, Tournus

new.title: Visit the Romanesque basilica of Paray-le-Monial
new.desc: The Basilique du Sacré-Coeur is a former Cluniac priory church often described as a small-scale model of Cluny III. It became a basilica in 1875 and is the most visited monument in Saône-et-Loire.
new.tip: Guided tours also take in the cloister and the historic centre.
new.q: Basilique du Sacré-Coeur, Avenue Jean-Paul II, Paray-le-Monial

new.title: Sit in the Church of Reconciliation at Taizé
new.desc: The ecumenical Taizé Community in the Saône-et-Loire hills built its Church of Reconciliation in 1961-62 with young German volunteers. Three daily prayers of song, readings and silence take place there.
new.tip: Visitors may attend the prayers; weekly stays need booking via taize.fr.
new.q: Église de la Réconciliation, Communauté de Taizé, Taizé

new.title: Explore the medieval village and castle of Brancion
new.desc: A walled village on a rocky spur with a castle built between the 11th and 13th centuries, a 16th-century covered market hall and the Romanesque Église Saint-Pierre with wall paintings. The keep gives a view over the plain.
new.tip: Park at the free car park 300 m away; the site is pedestrian only and tickets include an audioguide.
new.q: Château de Brancion, Martailly-lès-Brancion

new.title: Read Gislebertus's Last Judgment at Autun Cathedral
new.desc: The Cathédrale Saint-Lazare was built from about 1120 to house the relics of Saint Lazarus. Its tympanum of the Last Judgment, signed by Gislebertus, was rediscovered behind plaster in 1837.
new.tip: Look for the carved capitals inside, many by the same master, at eye level in the nave.
new.q: Cathédrale Saint-Lazare, Place du Terreau, Autun

new.title: Find Roman Augustodunum at the Porte d'Arroux
new.desc: The Porte d'Arroux is a 1st-century Roman gate, one of the two surviving in Autun, with Corinthian pilasters. Nearby on the Arroux road stands the Romano-Celtic tower called the Temple of Janus.
new.tip: The Roman theatre remains lie on the other side of town; the two sites combine in a loop walk.
new.q: Porte d'Arroux, Rue de la Croix Verte, Autun

new.title: Climb the great staircase of Château de Cormatin
new.desc: A 17th-century château with a grand open-well staircase more than 20 m high, tapestries and a boxwood maze leading to an aviary. The grounds cover about 11 hectares and include a kitchen garden of more than 90 species.
new.tip: Allow half a day for house and gardens.
new.q: Château de Cormatin, Cormatin

new.title: Visit the Musée Nicéphore Niépce in Chalon-sur-Saône
new.desc: Niépce created the first photograph in nearby Saint-Loup-de-Varennes around 1826-27, and Chalon's museum, founded in 1972, holds a vast photographic collection. The city is marking the bicentenary of photography with exhibitions.
new.tip: The museum stands on the quai des Messageries near the Île Saint-Laurent.
new.q: Musée Nicéphore Niépce, 28 Quai des Messageries, Chalon-sur-Saône

new.title: Discover the Schneider story at Château de la Verrerie
new.desc: A former royal crystal works turned into the Schneider family residence, today the Musée de l'Homme et de l'Industrie of the Écomusée Creusot-Montceau. It tells the story of the crystal works, the forges and the company town of Le Creusot.
new.tip: The main museum is free; the museum closes in December and January.
new.q: Château de la Verrerie, Le Creusot

new.title: See the Romanesque church in Semur-en-Brionnais
new.desc: The village is the birthplace of Saint Hugues, abbot of Cluny from 1049 to 1109. Its 12th-century collegiate church of Saint-Hilaire has a rare tympanum dedicated to Saint Hilary and has been listed since 1862.
new.tip: The village is a member of the most beautiful villages of France; climb to the castle area for views of the Brionnais.
new.q: Collégiale Saint-Hilaire, Semur-en-Brionnais

new.title: Spot the carved Maison de Bois in Mâcon
new.desc: The Maison de Bois dates from about 1490 and has a facade decorated with carved bas-reliefs. It is on the Place aux Herbes near the two Romanesque towers of the old Saint-Vincent cathedral and the Saône quays.
new.tip: Finish on the quays along the Saône; the Saturday morning market takes place by the Esplanade Lamartine.
new.q: Maison de Bois, Place aux Herbes, Mâcon

new.title: Eat œufs en meurette at Meurette & Persillé
new.desc: Chef Florent Colombo's casual counter at the Cité de la gastronomie makes the Burgundian poached eggs in red wine sauce its signature dish. It serves lunch every day and dinner from Thursday to Saturday without reservations.
new.tip: Order the œufs en meurette with the persillé; check hours before going as they differ by day.
new.q: Meurette & Persillé, 12 Parvis de l'Unesco, Dijon

new.title: Dine at the Michelin-starred Loiseau des Ducs
new.desc: A starred restaurant at 3 rue Vauban serving revisited Burgundian cuisine, with an egg yolk confit smoked with hay among the signature dishes. Tasting menus run roughly 40 to 120 euros before drinks.
new.tip: Reservation is essential; the lunch menu is the more affordable way in.
new.q: Loiseau des Ducs, 3 Rue Vauban, Dijon

new.title: Order escargots and meurette at La Fine Heure
new.desc: A bistro on rue Berbisey that offers a set menu of Burgundian specialities around 40 euros, including snails and œufs en meurette.
new.tip: Book in the evening; the Burgundian menu lists the classic dishes in one set.
new.q: La Fine Heure, 34 Rue Berbisey, Dijon

new.title: Buy pain d'épices at Mulot & Petitjean
new.desc: Founded in 1796, Mulot & Petitjean describes itself as the last pain d'épices factory in Dijon. Its storybook shop at place Bossuet sells gingerbread, mustard and nonnettes.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Saturday with a midday break; the factory at boulevard de l'Ouest has a small museum.
new.q: Mulot & Petitjean, 13 Place Bossuet, Dijon

new.title: Taste fresh-pumped mustard at the Maille boutique
new.desc: The Maille boutique at 32 rue de la Liberté sells mustards drawn from stoneware crocks, including white wine and truffle varieties. The Maille brand dates back to 1747.
new.tip: Confirm opening hours and whether the pump service is running before you go.
new.q: Maille, 32 Rue de la Liberté, Dijon

new.title: Eat your way round the Halles centrales market
new.desc: The covered market was built from 1873 to 1875 on the site of a former Dominican convent and has been a listed monument since 1975. It is open on market mornings and surrounded by restaurants and cafe terraces.
new.tip: Go on a Tuesday, Thursday, Friday or Saturday morning when the stalls are open.
new.q: Halles centrales de Dijon, Rue Bannelier, Dijon

new.title: Taste Anis de Flavigny in the old abbey
new.desc: The aniseed sweets have been made in the former Benedictine abbey of Flavigny-sur-Ozerain since the 16th century. The visit includes the production workshop, a small museum and the Carolingian crypt.
new.tip: Workshop tours run on weekday mornings; the shop is open longer hours.
new.q: Anis de Flavigny, 4 Rue de l'Abbaye, Flavigny-sur-Ozerain

new.title: Buy Cîteaux cheese at the abbey shop
new.desc: The monks of Cîteaux make a pressed farm cheese from the milk of their Montbéliarde cows, sold under that name since 1925. The abbey shop also sells monastic specialities such as honey sweets.
new.tip: The shop is closed Sunday morning and Monday; check that the cheese is back in production before going.
new.q: Boutique de l'Abbaye de Cîteaux, Saint-Nicolas-lès-Cîteaux

new.title: Taste Époisses at the Fromagerie Berthaut
new.desc: Robert and Simone Berthaut relaunched Époisses production in 1956 and their son Jean still runs the dairy. The washed-rind cheese is hand washed and ripened four weeks in several cellars; the Perrière was named best cheese in the world in 2023.
new.tip: Call or check the website for shop and visit hours before going.
new.q: Fromagerie Berthaut, Époisses

new.title: Splurge at La Côte d'Or by Bernard Loiseau
new.desc: The two-Michelin-star restaurant at the Relais Bernard Loiseau in Saulieu, the house where Bernard Loiseau cooked. Frog-leg jambonnettes remain a signature dish; there is also a more modest Bistrot Loiseau du Morvan.
new.tip: Book well ahead, or try the bistro for a cheaper taste of the house.
new.q: Relais Bernard Loiseau, 2 Avenue Bernard Loiseau, Saulieu

new.title: Eat Bresse chicken at L'Écrin de Yohann Chapuis in Tournus
new.desc: The former Restaurant Greuze, founded by Jean Ducloux, now holds one Michelin star under Yohann Chapuis and is known for Bresse poultry. The Bouchon Bourguignon bistro on the same premises serves a pâté en croûte and Bresse chicken with morels and vin jaune.
new.tip: Choose the bistro for a lower price; both sit by the abbey.
new.q: Restaurant Greuze, 1 Rue Albert Thibaudet, Tournus

new.title: Eat boeuf bourguignon at Ma Cuisine in Beaune
new.desc: A rustic bistro in the Passage Sainte-Hélène run by the Escoffier family, known for boeuf bourguignon, œufs en meurette and jambon persillé, with a deep Burgundy wine list.
new.tip: Evening service plus Friday lunch; reserve ahead.
new.q: Ma Cuisine, Passage Sainte-Hélène, Beaune

new.title: Try a praluline at Pralus in Beaune
new.desc: Pralus is a chocolatier known for the pink-almond praline brioche, the praluline. The Beaune shop is one of the family's boutiques.
new.tip: Take it as a snack on your walk between the Hospices and the collegiate church.
new.q: Pralus, Rue d'Alsace, Beaune

new.title: Pick up pastries at Fabien Berteau in Beaune
new.desc: A pâtisserie at 18 rue Monge near the market square, well regarded among Beaune's bakers for its cakes and viennoiseries.
new.tip: Buy a small tart or éclair for a picnic by the ramparts.
new.q: Pâtisserie Fabien Berteau, 18 Rue Monge, Beaune

new.title: Visit the Fallot mustard mill in Beaune
new.desc: Moutarderie Fallot is a Burgundy mustard maker with a mill at 31 rue du Faubourg Bretonniere in Beaune. It offers two guided visit routes and a workshop shop.
new.tip: Book a visit in advance and buy a jar at the shop.
new.q: Moutarderie Fallot, 31 Rue du Faubourg Bretonnière, Beaune

new.title: Dine at Restaurant Pierre in Mâcon
new.desc: A Michelin-starred restaurant at 7-9 rue Joseph Dufour in the centre, led by Jacky Tauvry with classic regional cooking, short supply chains and seasonal dishes.
new.tip: Book ahead; ask for Mâconnais wines by the glass.
new.q: Restaurant Pierre, 7-9 Rue Joseph Dufour, Mâcon

new.title: Lunch at Ma Table en Ville in Mâcon
new.desc: A more affordable Michelin Plate restaurant on rue de Strasbourg, with modern cooking at mid-range prices.
new.tip: Reserve for dinner; the lunch menu is the best value.
new.q: Ma Table en Ville, 50 Rue de Strasbourg, Mâcon

new.title: Taste Morvan specialities at Le Petit Rolin in Autun
new.desc: A bistronomic restaurant in Autun serving Morvan and Burgundy specialities, with a view of the cathedral.
new.tip: Ask for the daily special; it is close to Saint-Lazare for an after-visit meal.
new.q: Le Petit Rolin, Rue Cocand, Autun

new.title: Follow the Owl Trail through old Dijon
new.desc: A marked walking circuit of 22 sites in the historic centre, indicated by owl silhouettes set into the pavement. It starts at the tourist office and passes townhouses, Notre-Dame with its Jacquemart, the lucky owl and the Maison Millière.
new.tip: Pick up the free leaflet at the tourist office on rue des Forges; allow about two hours.
new.q: Office de tourisme de Dijon, 11 Rue des Forges, Dijon

new.title: Climb the 316 steps of the Tour Philippe le Bon
new.desc: A 46-metre tower built around 1450-60 for Duke Philip the Good, rising above the ducal palace. At the top there is a 360-degree view over Dijon's tiled roofs and the vineyards.
new.tip: Visits are guided only and must be booked at the tourist office; groups are limited to 18.
new.q: Tour Philippe le Bon, Place de la Libération, Dijon

new.title: Browse the Halles market on a market morning
new.desc: Dijon's covered market, built in the 1870s with iron pavilions, trades on Tuesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday mornings. Stalls and surrounding streets sell Burgundy cheeses, charcuterie and wine.
new.tip: Saturday is the biggest day with the outdoor forain market around the hall.
new.q: Les Halles, Rue Bannelier, Dijon

new.title: Swim or stroll at Lac Kir
new.desc: A man-made lake west of the centre with supervised swimming beaches in summer and a path around its shore. Dijon Plage sets up deckchairs along the beaches each summer.
new.tip: Check the water-quality reports before swimming; the lake is free and open in summer.
new.q: Lac Kir, Dijon

new.title: Cycle the Canal de Bourgogne towpath from Dijon
new.desc: The Tour de Bourgogne cycle route follows the canal out of Dijon to Plombières-lès-Dijon, about 3.5 km, then 5 km of towpath to Velars-sur-Ouche. Plombières has a church with a glazed-tile spire.
new.tip: The section is busy with families, so keep speed moderate; the A38 motorway runs near the canal in places.
new.q: Port du Canal, Dijon

new.title: Graze at the Foire internationale et gastronomique de Dijon
new.desc: The annual fair at the Parc des Expositions runs over twelve days, from 31 October to 11 November in 2026, mixing trade stands with regional food and wine.
new.tip: Entry is paid by day ticket and cheaper after 6 pm outside late-night openings.
new.q: Parc des Expositions et Congrès, Dijon

new.title: Taste crème de cassis at the Cassissium
new.desc: A museum in Nuits-Saint-Georges on the blackcurrant, with a guided tour of the neighbouring Védrenne liqueur factory and a tasting of crème de cassis, liqueurs and syrups.
new.tip: Hours vary by day and it is closed Sunday; check the official site.
new.q: Le Cassissium, 8 Passage Montgolfier, Nuits-Saint-Georges

new.title: Taste Pommard at Château de Pommard
new.desc: The château offers an hour-long Clos Marey-Monge tasting of six Pommard reds, including three from neighbouring biodynamic plots that show how soil changes the wine. It is offered in English and French.
new.tip: Book in advance; the host manages the calendar.
new.q: Château de Pommard, 15 Rue Marey-Monge, Pommard

new.title: Visit the cellars of Château de Meursault
new.desc: Guided tours cover vast underground caves, the oldest dating to the 12th century, including a 500 sq m 16th-century cellar. The château hosts the Paulée the day after the Hospices de Beaune auction.
new.tip: Book several weeks ahead; visits with tasting take about two hours.
new.q: Château de Meursault, Rue Moulin Foulot, Meursault

new.title: Walk the Patriarche cellars with six wines
new.desc: The cellars of Patriarche Père et Fils in a former Visitandines convent are billed as Burgundy's largest wine cellars. The Liberté visit is an audio-guided tour of about an hour with six Burgundy wines to taste.
new.tip: Each November the house runs a wine sale weekend with special tastings.
new.q: Caves Patriarche Père & Fils, 5 Rue du Collège, Beaune

new.title: Cycle the Voie des Vignes from Beaune to Santenay
new.desc: A signposted route of about 23 km on small roads and vineyard tracks through Pommard, Meursault and Chassagne to Santenay. Train stations at Beaune, Meursault, Chagny and Santenay allow shorter rides.
new.tip: Rent bikes in Beaune; a continuation from Santenay runs along the Canal du Centre towpath.
new.q: Voie des Vignes, Parc de la Bouzaise, Beaune

new.title: Climb the Roche de Solutré
new.desc: A Grand Site de France where a marked trail climbs to the limestone crest above the Pouilly-Fuissé vineyards, about 200,000 people a year. At the foot the Musée de Préhistoire covers a site occupied for more than 50,000 years.
new.tip: Access to the rock is free while the museum charges admission; the climb suits families but not wheelchairs.
new.q: Maison du Grand Site, Roche de Solutré, Solutré-Pouilly

new.title: Taste Pouilly-Fuissé at Domaines Auvigue
new.desc: Domaines Auvigue settled in the former church of Fuissé, converted into a winemaking and tasting-sale space. The domain offers visits with tasting of its Pouilly-Fuissé and other Mâconnais wines.
new.tip: Book a slot; tastings last about half an hour.
new.q: Domaines Auvigue, Fuissé

new.title: Ride the Voie Verte from Cluny to Givry
new.desc: France's first greenway opened in 1997 on an old railway line between Givry and Cluny, extended in 2005 and 2007. A 14 km extension past the Bois Clair tunnel reaches Charnay-lès-Mâcon.
new.tip: The Cluny to Mâcon stretch is considered the most scenic; trains with bike space serve Chalon and Mâcon.
new.q: Voie Verte, Gare de Cluny, Cluny

new.title: Browse the Monday market under the Louhans arcades
new.desc: Louhans' traditional market takes place on Monday mornings, with around 250 vendors spread under the arcades of the Grande Rue, including Bresse poultry. Each December the Glorieuses de Bresse poultry competitions are held in the town.
new.tip: Go early on Monday morning; arcades keep you dry in rain.
new.q: Grande Rue, Louhans

new.title: Browse the Saturday market on the Mâcon quays
new.desc: The big open-air Saturday market takes place on the Esplanade Lamartine on the Saône quays, close to the Maison de Bois and the Saint-Vincent towers.
new.tip: Arrive before noon and picnic on the quay.
new.q: Esplanade Lamartine, Mâcon

new.title: Join the Carnaval de Chalon-sur-Saône
new.desc: Chalon's February carnival fills the streets with parades, elaborate costumes and revelry around the Place Saint-Vincent and the old town.
new.tip: Check exact dates on the Chalon tourism site.
new.q: Place Saint-Vincent, Chalon-sur-Saône
